read: partial: main text pp. 1-9 in full (abstract, introduction, related work, dataset construction, experiments, error analysis, conclusion, statements); appendix B with Tables S1-S2 (pp. 14-15) and D.1 (p. 21) read, and the data-collection note at the end of appendix A (p. 14); prompt and example appendices not read
venue_now: ICML 2024, PMLR 235 (p. 1 footer); the file is arXiv 2307.10635v3, 28 Jun 2024
what_it_is: A benchmark of college-level scientific problem solving: 869 free-response problems from ten widely used physics, chemistry and mathematics textbooks, 177 of them with visual context, plus a closed set of 103 problems from seven computer-science and mathematics course exams (p. 2, p. 4). Textbook answers are single numbers, graded against the reference within a 5% relative tolerance; exam answers are graded with the instructors' rubrics (p. 5). A minority of problems carry step-by-step reference solutions, which feed an error analysis in which annotators locate the faulty line and an LLM verifier attributes errors to ten problem-solving skills (p. 4, p. 7-8). The best configuration, GPT-4 with Python, scores 43.22% on the textbook set (p. 2, p. 6).
domain: college-level physics (Fundamentals of Physics, Statistical Thermodynamics, Classical Dynamics), chemistry (quantum and physical chemistry) and mathematics (calculus, statistics, differential equations) from textbooks; computer science and mathematics course exams (p. 2, p. 4)
size: 869 textbook problems (physics 291, chemistry 269, mathematics 309 by Table 2, p. 4; 177 with visual context, p. 2) and 103 closed exam problems from seven midterms and finals (p. 2; Table S1, p. 15); seven unimodal LLMs on the textbook set (p. 5) and multimodal models on the visual subset (p. 7)
source_of_items: textbooks (ten college textbooks, Table 2, p. 4) and course exams (Data Mining, Machine Learning and Differential Equations midterms and finals, Table S1, p. 15), extracted manually from PDF into LaTeX with Mathpix (p. 5)
has_gold_traces: partial: detailed step-by-step LaTeX solutions for 9.1% to 21.5% of each textbook's problems (Table 2, p. 4; about 138 of 869 by my arithmetic), used for few-shot examples and error analysis (p. 5, p. 7), not for grading
evaluation: final answer: textbook answers are single numbers rounded to three decimal places with units stored separately, accepted within a 5% relative tolerance; exam answers graded with instructors' rubrics (p. 5). Separately, an LLM verifier attributes each wrong answer to one of ten skills for error profiles, which is analysis, not scoring (p. 7-8)
human_validation: Problems were collected by seven annotators, one to two textbooks each (p. 14), and checked to compile in LaTeX (p. 5); code snippets for the tool setting were verified by annotators (p. 5). Error analysis: two college students marked the faulty line and its cause in 112 GPT-3.5 errors (p. 7); the GPT-3.5 verifier's skill attributions were checked by two annotators on 151 samples, 123 correct (81.45%) (p. 21), and about 20% of attributions were discarded (p. 8). No validation of the 5% answer grader is reported.
contamination_measures: problems extracted manually from PDF textbooks and chosen for 'inaccessibility in text formats' to limit leakage (p. 2, p. 4); a closed exam set that is 'less likely to be in LLM training data' (p. 2, p. 4)

engtrace_use.sentence: R-1 (July 2026 rebuttal; SciBench is not cited in the May paper): 'SciBench (Wang et al., 2023) allows a 5% relative tolerance for grading numeric answers on college-level scientific problems'
engtrace_use.explanation: The claim matches the paper for the textbook set: 'we compare the model outputs with the correct answers, allowing a relative tolerance of 5%' (p. 5), on college-level physics, chemistry and mathematics problems (p. 1-2). Two qualifications: exam answers are graded with instructors' rubrics rather than the tolerance (p. 5), and textbook answers are rounded to three decimals with units stored separately before comparison (p. 5). The key 'Wang et al., 2023' does not match the version in the file, which is ICML 2024 (p. 1 footer), and it collides with NEWTON's key (Wang et al., 2023) in the May reference list.

suggested_wording: SciBench (Wang et al., 2024) collects 869 free-response problems from ten college physics, chemistry and mathematics textbooks and grades their numerical answers within a 5% relative tolerance; reference solutions accompany only a minority of problems and serve error analysis rather than grading.
facts_to_cite: 869 free-response problems from ten college textbooks, physics 291, chemistry 269 and mathematics 309 (Table 2, p. 4; sums mine), 177 of them with visual context (p. 2), plus a closed set of 103 problems from seven computer-science and mathematics exams (p. 2).

Textbook answers are single numbers rounded to three decimals with units stored separately, graded against the reference within a 5% relative tolerance; exam answers are graded with instructors' rubrics (p. 5).
Step-by-step reference solutions are provided for 9.1% to 21.5% of each textbook's problems (Table 2, p. 4).
Problems were extracted manually from PDFs into LaTeX and chosen to be hard to find in text form, to limit training-data leakage (p. 2, p. 4).
The best textbook score is 43.22%, by GPT-4 with Python tools (p. 2, p. 6).

Error analysis: two annotators located the faulty line in 112 GPT-3.5 solutions; the errors were distilled into ten skills, and a GPT-3.5 verifier then attributed wrong answers to skills, with 123 of 151 attributions judged correct by two annotators (81.45%) (p. 7-8, p. 21).
Its authors name engineering among the subjects the benchmark does not yet cover (p. 9).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: college-level quantitative free-response problems graded within a numeric tolerance (5% here; EngTrace uses REL 0.002 or one unit of the last digit, state brief section 2), with units handled separately (p. 5); thermodynamics and physical-chemistry content that overlaps EngTrace's chemical branch (Table 2, p. 4); step-by-step reference solutions for a minority of problems (p. 4); line-level human annotation of where a model's solution goes wrong (p. 7) and an LLM verifier whose labels were checked by humans (p. 21), the nearest thing here to EngTrace's step labels and validated judge. Lacks: generated instances (fixed textbook items); gold traces for every item; step-level scoring (the verifier only profiles errors after grading, p. 7-8); an engineering setting (named by the authors as future work, p. 9); validation of the answer grader (the 81.45% check concerns the error classifier, not the grader).
notes: Not in the May paper; used only in the July rebuttal (R-1), whose 5% claim is accurate for the textbook set (p. 5). Cite the ICML 2024 version (p. 1) as Wang et al., 2024 to avoid a clash with NEWTON (Wang et al., 2023). 'Must' rests on three points: it is the standard college-level science benchmark with numeric tolerance grading, the rebuttal already relied on it, and it shares chemistry and thermodynamics content with EngTrace; the must-versus-should call is a judgement (medium confidence), the facts are not. Internal inconsistency in the paper: the best exam score is 51.57% on p. 2 and 57.54% on p. 7; Table S2 (p. 15) gives GPT-4 with zero-shot CoT a mean per-exam score of 51.57% (my arithmetic). The exam set also contains multiple-choice and true-false items (Table S1, p. 15), so 'all open-ended' (p. 2) holds for the textbook set only. Belongs in the physical-sciences paragraph and beside EngTrace's tolerance choice in the evaluation section; its error-profiling protocol is also citable in the judge-validity paragraph as a small human check of an LLM classifier.
